full_article:
This piece was adapted from an earlier Stimson Center Commentary, “ A Cascading Disaster on the China–Nepal Border: What to Know About the August 2026 Rasuwa Flood, 72 Hours Later , ” and updated to reflect current conditions.



On August 26, 2026, a massive volume of bedrock and glacial ice broke loose 5,200 meters above sea level on the north side of Nepal’s Langtang range, triggering a “rock-ice avalanche” that crashed into the Lhende River on the Nepal-China border fueling the deadliest extreme flow disaster on record in the country. This cascade barreled downstream at an average of ~160 kilometers per hour downstream toward the Nepal-China border. It slammed into and overwhelmed Chinese border facilities at Rasuwagadhi just 7.5 minutes after the mountain gave way, then tore across the border and down the Bhotekoshi/Trishuli River corridor into Nepal, swallowing towns and causing extensive damage over 100 kilometers from its source.

As of 2:00pm ET on September 3rd a total of 1,259 people are confirmed dead and over 5,000 people are still reported missing. These numbers include Nepalis living and working along the river corridor, hundreds of foreign tourists visiting the Langtang region and pilgrims crossing to Mount Kailash, and hundreds of hydropower workers trapped in tunnels. The border town of Timure and the market hub of Syaphrubesi were essentially wiped away; 19 bridges and 40 kilometers of highway are gone, and more than 430 megawatts of hydropower capacity, representing more than 10% of Nepal’s national supply, is offline.

Cropped from Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi Flood: Search, Rescue and Relief Response, Situation Response #3 , Issued September 3, 2026. Source: National Disaster Risk Reduction & Management Authority (NDRRMA), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of Nepal

The residents of Nepal’s Rasuwa district, which includes a large Tamang population, have lived with disaster risk (e.g. floods, landslides, earthquakes, and avalanches) for centuries and they have adapted to and managed these risks. But the risks are changing fast, and the level of exposure communities face today is unprecedented.

I say this, having spent nearly 14 years conducting research in this river basin (in all of the affected settlements in Rasuwa), having led post-disaster relief activities in many of these towns after the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, and having personally survived a massive glacier avalanche on the other side of the very same mountain, which led to years of research and direct engagement. None of this is abstract to me, and my heart breaks for Rasuwa again.

A Cascade, Not a Rainfall Disaster

This catastrophic event happened on a clear day. Unlike many of Nepal’s recent disasters, it wasn’t triggered by extreme rainfall or an earthquake, and surprisingly, given the volume of water, there wasn’t a lake involved. Post-event analysis points to an unexpected culprit: the sheer force of the rock-ice avalanche that became more flood-like as it gathered water, rock, and sediment and funneled through the Trishuli’s tight canyons, arriving downstream as a fast-moving wall of concrete. This was a single, continuous, cascading extreme flow event.

Figure 1: Map of the impacted areas with timestamps for flood propagation (Source: CLaSH, Accessed September 2, 2026)

Scientists are still working to establish whether climate change played a role in destabilizing the source area, and formal processes of evaluating attribution are now underway. But the frequency of extreme flow events in recent years suggests that climate change is destabilizing the mountain cryosphere across the Himalayan region. Simply put, warming and climatic volatility can impact glaciers, weaken permafrost, and drive rapid or unseasonal changes in snowpack. In Nepal, climate-related risks interact with monsoon dynamics and seismic risk to compound danger in ways that existing monitoring frameworks aren’t built to see.

This event joins a grim and growing list of Himalayan cascading disasters — the 2021 Chamoli flood, the 2021 Melamchi disaster, the 2023 South Lhonak GLOF (Glacial Lake Outburst Flow), and the 2025 Blatten collapse in Switzerland. Notably, a smaller glacial flood struck this exact watershed in July 2025, destroying the same border bridge and killing 19 people — a warning sign that didn’t translate into readiness for what came next.

Of Blind Spots and Needles in Haystacks

It would be wrong to read this as a failure of Nepal’s early warning systems. The source area sits in a genuine gap — a narrow sliver of unpopulated Nepali territory that drains north into China, falling between the scientific attention long focused on the south side of the Langtang range and the Chinese monitoring effort that intensified after last year’s flood. Nepal’s gauge and station networks were built to catch monsoon floods and glacial lake outbursts, not a catastrophic flow that outran any possible alert. But generating alerts for an event like this isn’t just a problem of data scarcity or blind spots, it’s also a problem of speed and scale. The Himalaya has more slopes capable of failing this catastrophically, across more vertical relief, than anywhere else on Earth. Scientists can and have highlighted a variety of high-risk areas and landforms, but finding subtle changes in a timely fashion requires skillfully separating signal from noise as risk changes across the Himalaya.

The overall point is that experts need a signal to effectively direct their tools and attention – and finding these signals can often feel like finding needles in Himalaya haystacks. Of roughly a dozen extreme flow events in the region over the past decade, only one — the 2023 South Lhonak outburst — struck a site already flagged as risky. Every other event originated from somewhere no one was watching, including this one.

Learning from Disasters Like This

Each event offers lessons and insights that allow us to return with greater precision and a new understanding of where similar hazard chains might be stacking up. For example, the 2024 Thame (GLOF) taught researchers that small glacial lakes can grow dangerously fast; last year’s transboundary flood event along the same Lhende River into Rasuwa showed that supraglacial lakes — lakes on top of glaciers — can expand and drain catastrophically. Last week’s event highlights the increasing prevalence of another kind of risk: showing how an ice-rock avalanche can trigger a massive flood-like event and impact communities more than 100 kilometers downstream.

Tools are rapidly developing, but no single instrument will catch everything, so the approach has to be layered — weather stations and river gauges as a foundation, satellite monitoring to track remote terrain, seismic networks to triangulate a failure within seconds, and, critically, local observers such as herders, mountaineers, and fishers who can flag a crack or a filling lake long before a sensor does. Even a few minutes of warning can be the difference between an evacuation and a recovery operation.

What the Stimson Nepal Early Warning Team is Doing

In the wake of this event, on the Stimson Center’s Early Warning for Cascading Disasters in Nepal project team, working in Nepal and Washington, rapidly mobilized to assess the event, gather information, and share expert analysis with Government of Nepal institutions such as the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) and government hydrologists and meteorologists. Using Sentinel-1, Landsat, and Planet Labs imagery, we identified the avalanche’s source, ruled out a supraglacial lake we had assessed last year, and confirmed the landslide-dam mechanism. We also tasked commercial radar/SAR imagery from ICEYE US over the source and blockage sites and delivered pre- and post-event comparisons to NDRRMA and Nepal’s Home Ministry within hours.

After two new lakes formed in the avalanche flowpath — one along the Lhende River, another high in the upper catchment — we worked with the NDRRMA to assess changing conditions, analyze breach scenarios, and provide scientific analysis of the flood pulses that came when the lake began to finally drain on August 30th. Members of our team also contributed to the HIRISK rapid assessment, prepared by an international group of Chinese, Nepali, American, Austrian, Swiss, and Dutch scientists, which was published on August 28.

Lingering Risks and Uncertainties, in Both Nepal and China

Risks remain throughout the region, and heavy rain could still reactivate destabilized slopes or remobilize other landforms within the impacted area. Critically, the monsoon season is not yet over. There are risks that we know of, such as risks from specific glacial lakes in China. But we can’t discount the risks we are not yet aware of from other potential cascading hazards. Monitoring these risks often requires both focused efforts on high-risk areas and triaging between uncertainties.

In this wake of this devastating event, we are already seeing better transboundary coordination between Nepal and China. High-priority information is being shared and new channels of communication opened between Chinese and Nepali authorities — a promising, if overdue, shift. A variety of people have called for greater formal coordination and the establishment of transboundary monitoring networks.

To be clear, no one — not Nepal, not China, not the international scientific community — could have identified the subtle changes and specific risks that triggered this disaster. Forensic analysis is yielding new insights that we can use to search for similar risks in the future, but this event began with a sudden mass movement that turned into an extreme flow far too fast for a true alert to be shared. The hope is that this disaster will catalyze the kind of sustained, cross-border monitoring and cooperation the region has needed for years.

नेपाल केरऽ रसुवा जिला केरऽ निवासी, जेकरा म॑ तामांग केरऽ एगो बड़ऽ आबादी शामिल छै, सदियो स॑ आपदा केरऽ जोखिम (जैना बाढ़, भूस्खलन, भूकंप, आरू हिमस्खलन) के साथ जी रहलऽ छै आरू वू ई जोखिमऽ के अनुकूल होय गेलऽ छै आरू ओकरऽ प्रबंधन करी चुकलऽ छै । लेकिन जोखिम तेजी स॑ बदली रहलऽ छै, आरू आज समुदायऽ क॑ जेतना एक्सपोजर के सामना करना पड़ै छै, वू अभूतपूर्व छै ।

हम ई बात कहैत छी, लगभग 14 साल एहि नदी बेसिन में (रसुवा के सब प्रभावित बस्ती में) शोध करय में बितेलहुं, 2015 के गोरखा भूकंप के बाद एहि में सं बहुतो शहर में आपदा के बाद राहत गतिविधि के नेतृत्व केने छी, आ व्यक्तिगत रूप सं ठीक ओही पहाड़ के दोसर कात एकटा विशाल ग्लेशियर हिमस्खलन सं बचलहुं, जाहि सं सालों सं शोध आ प्रत्यक्ष संलग्नता भेल. एहि मे सँ कोनो बात हमरा लेल अमूर्त नहि अछि, आ हमर मोन फेर रसुवा लेल टूटि जाइत अछि।

एकटा झरना, बरखाक आपदा नहि

ई विनाशकारी घटना साफ दिन मे घटित भेल। नेपाल केरऽ हाल केरऽ बहुत आपदा के विपरीत ई अत्यधिक वर्षा या भूकंप स॑ नै शुरू होय गेलऽ छेलै, आरू आश्चर्य के बात छै कि पानी केरऽ मात्रा क॑ देखत॑ हुअ॑ एकरा म॑ कोनो झील नै छेलै । घटना के बाद के विश्लेषण एकटा अप्रत्याशित अपराधी दिस इशारा करैत अछि : चट्टान-बर्फ के हिमस्खलन के सरासर बल जे पानि, चट्टान आ तलछट के जमा करैत बाढ़ि सन बेसी भ गेल आ त्रिशुली के कड़ा घाटी में फनल करैत, कंक्रीटक तेजी सं चलैत देबाल के रूप में नीचा पहुंचैत. ई एकटा एकल, निरंतर, झरना-झरना चरम प्रवाहक घटना छल ।

चित्र 1: बाढ़ प्रसार कें लेल समय मुहर कें साथ प्रभावित क्षेत्रक कें नक्शा (स्रोत: CLaSH, अभिगमन तिथि 2 सितंबर, 2026)

वैज्ञानिक सब अखनी भी ई स्थापित करै के काम करी रहलऽ छै कि जलवायु परिवर्तन न॑ स्रोत क्षेत्र क॑ अस्थिर करै म॑ भूमिका निभैलकै कि नै, आरू अब॑ एट्रिब्यूशन के मूल्यांकन के औपचारिक प्रक्रिया चलैलऽ जाय रहलऽ छै । लेकिन हाल के सालऽ म॑ चरम प्रवाह के घटना के आवृत्ति स॑ ई बात के संकेत मिलै छै कि जलवायु परिवर्तन पूरा हिमालयी क्षेत्र म॑ पहाड़ी क्रायोस्फीयर क॑ अस्थिर करी रहलऽ छै । सीधा शब्दऽ म॑ कहलऽ जाय त॑ गर्मी आरू जलवायु अस्थिरता ग्लेशियर प॑ प्रभाव डाल॑ सकै छै, परमाफ्रॉस्ट क॑ कमजोर करी सकै छै आरू स्नोपैक म॑ तेजी स॑ या गैर-मौसम परिवर्तन क॑ बढ़ावा द॑ सकै छै । नेपाल मे जलवायु सं जुड़ल जोखिम मानसून गतिशीलता आ भूकंपीय जोखिम कें साथ बातचीत करयत छै आ खतरा कें बढ़ाबै छै जे मौजूदा निगरानी ढाँचा देखय कें लेल नहि बनायल गेल छै.

ई घटना हिमालय केरऽ झरना वाला आपदा केरऽ एगो भयावह आरू बढ़तऽ सूची म॑ शामिल होय जाय छै — २०२१ केरऽ चमोली बाढ़, २०२१ केरऽ मेलमची आपदा, २०२३ केरऽ साउथ ल्होनक जीएलओएफ (ग्लेशियल लेक आउटबर्स्ट फ्लो), आरू २०२५ म॑ स्विट्जरलैंड म॑ ब्लैटन केरऽ पतन । उल्लेखनीय छै कि जुलाई 2025 म॑ ई सटीक जल-विभाजन म॑ एगो छोटऽ हिमनदी बाढ़ आबी गेलै, जेकरा म॑ वही सीमा पुल क॑ नष्ट करी देलऽ गेलै आरू 19 लोगऽ के मौत होय गेलै — एगो चेतावनी संकेत जेकरऽ अनुवाद आगू की होतै ओकरा लेली तत्परता म॑ नै बदललै ।

घास के ढेर में अंधा धब्बे एवं सुई के

एकरा नेपाल केरऽ पूर्व चेतावनी प्रणाली केरऽ विफलता के रूप म॑ पढ़ना गलत होतै । स्रोत क्षेत्र एगो वास्तविक अंतराल म॑ बैठलऽ छै — अजनबी नेपाली इलाका केरऽ एगो संकीर्ण टुकड़ा जे उत्तर तरफ चीन म॑ बह॑ छै, जे लंबा समय स॑ लैंगटांग श्रृंखला केरऽ दक्षिणी तरफ केंद्रित वैज्ञानिक ध्यान आरू चीनी निगरानी प्रयास के बीच गिरै छै जे पिछला साल केरऽ बाढ़ के बाद तेज होय गेलऽ छै । नेपाल केरऽ गेज आरू स्टेशन नेटवर्क मानसून केरऽ बाढ़ आरू हिमनदी झील केरऽ विस्फोट क॑ पकड़ै लेली बनलऽ छेलै, नै कि कोनो भी संभावित अलर्ट स॑ आगू बढ़ै वाला विनाशकारी प्रवाह । मुदा एहि तरहक इवेंट के लेल अलर्ट जेनरेट करब सिर्फ डाटा के कमी या ब्लाइंड स्पॉट के समस्या नहिं अछि, ई स्पीड आओर स्केल के सेहो समस्या अछि. हिमालय केरऽ ढलान पृथ्वी केरऽ अन्य जगहऽ स॑ भी अधिक ढलान छै जे एकरा विनाशकारी रूप स॑ विफल करै म॑ सक्षम छै, अधिक ऊर्ध्वाधर राहत के पार । वैज्ञानिकऽ न॑ विभिन्न प्रकार के उच्च जोखिम वाला क्षेत्र आरू भू-रूप क॑ उजागर करी सकै छै आरू करी चुकलऽ छै, लेकिन समय प॑ सूक्ष्म परिवर्तन खोजै लेली हिमालय भर म॑ जोखिम म॑ बदलाव के साथ-साथ संकेत क॑ शोर स॑ कुशलता स॑ अलग करै के जरूरत छै ।

समग्र बात ई छै कि विशेषज्ञऽ क॑ अपनऽ औजार आरू ध्यान क॑ प्रभावी ढंग स॑ निर्देशित करै लेली एगो संकेत के जरूरत छै – आरू ई संकेतऽ क॑ खोजना अक्सर हिमालय केरऽ घास के ढेर म॑ सुई खोजै के तरह महसूस होय सकै छै । पिछला एक दशक मँ ई क्षेत्र मँ लगभग एक दर्जन चरम प्रवाह घटना मँ सँ केवल एक - २०२३ केरौ दक्षिण ल्होनाक विस्फोट - एगो ऐसनौ जगह प हमला करलकै जेकरा पहिने सँ जोखिम भरलौ के रूप मँ चिन्हित करलौ गेलौ छेलै । आन सभ आयोजन कतहु सँ उत्पन्न भेल छल जतय कियो नहि देखैत छल, जाहि मे ई आयोजन सेहो शामिल छल ।

एहि तरहक आपदा स सीखब

प्रत्येक आयोजन सबक आ अंतर्दृष्टि प्रदान करयत छै जे हमरा बेसि परिशुद्धता आ एकटा नव समझ कें साथ वापस आवय कें अनुमति देयत छै की समान खतरा श्रृंखला कतय ढेर भ सकय छै. जेना, 2024 केरऽ टेम (GLOF) न॑ शोधकर्ता सिनी क॑ सिखाबै छेलै कि छोटऽ-छोटऽ हिमनदी झील खतरनाक रूप स॑ तेजी स॑ बढ़ी सकै छै ; पिछला साल वही ल्हेंडे नदी के किनारे रसुवा में सीमा पार के बाढ़ के घटना स॑ पता चललै कि सुप्रैग्लेशियल झील — ग्लेशियर के ऊपर झील — विस्तार करी सकै छै आरू विनाशकारी रूप स॑ पानी निकासी करी सकै छै । पिछला सप्ताह केरऽ ई आयोजन एगो आरू तरह के जोखिम के बढ़तऽ प्रसार प॑ प्रकाश डालै छै: ई देखाबै छै कि कोना बर्फ-चट्टानऽ के हिमस्खलन एगो बड़ऽ बाढ़ जैसनऽ घटना क॑ शुरू करी सकै छै आरू 100 किलोमीटर स॑ भी अधिक नीचें के समुदायऽ प॑ प्रभाव डाल॑ सकै छै ।

उपकरण तेजी स॑ विकसित होय रहलऽ छै, लेकिन कोय भी एक उपकरण सब कुछ नै पकड़तै, ई लेली ई दृष्टिकोण क॑ परतदार बनाबै ल॑ पड़तै — मौसम स्टेशन आरू नदी गेज क॑ नींव के रूप म॑, दूरस्थ इलाका क॑ ट्रैक करै लेली उपग्रह निगरानी, ​​सेकंड के भीतर विफलता क॑ त्रिकोणीय करै लेली भूकंपीय नेटवर्क, आरू, महत्वपूर्ण रूप स॑, स्थानीय पर्यवेक्षक जेना कि चरवाहा, पर्वतारोही, आरू मछुआरा जे कोनो सेंसर स॑ बहुत पहलें दरार या भरना झील क॑ झंडा देखा सकै छै । किछ मिनटक कें चेतावनी कें सेहो निकासी आ रिकवरी ऑपरेशन कें बीच अंतर भ सकएय छै.

स्टिमसन नेपाल पूर्व चेतावनी दल की क रहल अछि

ई आयोजन के मद्देनजर नेपाल आरू वाशिंगटन म॑ काम करै वाला स्टिमसन सेंटर केरऽ नेपाल म॑ झरना वाला आपदा लेली प्रारंभिक चेतावनी परियोजना टीम प॑ तेजी स॑ आयोजन के आकलन करै, जानकारी जुटाबै, आरू नेपाल सरकार केरऽ संस्थान जेना कि राष्ट्रीय आपदा जोखिम कम करै आरू प्रबंधन प्राधिकरण (एनडीआरआरएएमए) आरू सरकारी जलविज्ञानी आरू मौसम वैज्ञानिकऽ के साथ विशेषज्ञ विश्लेषण साझा करै लेली जुटलऽ छेलै । सेंटिनल-1, लैंडसैट, आरू प्लैनेट लैब केरऽ इमेजरी के उपयोग करी क॑ हम्मं॑ हिमस्खलन केरऽ स्रोत के पहचान करलियै, पिछला साल हम्मं॑ आकलन करलऽ गेलऽ सुप्रैग्लेशियल झील क॑ खारिज करी देल॑ छेलियै आरू भूस्खलन-डैम तंत्र के पुष्टि करल॑ छेलियै । हम स्रोत आरू रुकावट स्थल के ऊपर आईसीईई यूएस स॑ वाणिज्यिक रडार/एसएआर इमेजरी क॑ भी काम सौंपलकै आरू घंटऽ के भीतर एनडीआरआरएएमए आरू नेपाल केरऽ गृह मंत्रालय क॑ घटना स॑ पहल॑ आरू बाद के तुलना पहुँचैलकै ।

हिमस्खलन प्रवाहमार्ग में दू टा नव झील बनलाक बाद - एकटा ल्हेन्डे नदीक कात, दोसर ऊपरी जलग्रहण क्षेत्र में ऊँच - हम एनडीआरआरएएमए के संग मिलिकय बदलैत परिस्थिति के आकलन केलहुं, उल्लंघन के परिदृश्य के विश्लेषण केलहुं, आ बाढ़ के दाल के वैज्ञानिक विश्लेषण उपलब्ध करौलहुं जे 30 अगस्त के अंततः झील में पानी निकलय लागल. हमरऽ टीम के सदस्यऽ न॑ चीनी, नेपाली, अमेरिकी, ऑस्ट्रियाई, स्विस, आरू डच वैज्ञानिकऽ के एगो अंतर्राष्ट्रीय समूह द्वारा तैयार करलऽ गेलऽ HIRISK रैपिड आकलन म॑ भी योगदान देलकै, जे २८ अगस्त क॑ प्रकाशित करलऽ गेलऽ छेलै ।

विलम्बित जोखिम आ अनिश्चितता, नेपाल आ चीन दुनू मे

पूरा क्षेत्र म॑ जोखिम बनलऽ छै, आरू भारी बारिश स॑ अखनी भी अस्थिर ढलान क॑ पुनः सक्रिय करलऽ जाब॑ सकै छै या प्रभावित क्षेत्र के भीतर अन्य भू-रूप क॑ पुनः गतिशील करलऽ जाब॑ सकै छै । आलोचनात्मक रूप स मानसून क मौसम एखन खत्म नहि भेल अछि। जोखिम छै जे हमरा सब क॑ पता छै, जेना कि चीन केरऽ विशिष्ट हिमनदी झीलऽ स॑ जोखिम । मुदा हम सब ओहि जोखिम कें छूट नहि द’ सकैत छी जकर जानकारी हमरा सब कें एखन धरि नहिं अछि, अन्य संभावित झरना खतरा सं. अइ जोखिम कें निगरानी कें लेल अक्सर उच्च जोखिम वाला क्षेत्रक पर केंद्रित प्रयास आ अनिश्चितताक कें बीच परीक्षण दूनू कें आवश्यकता होयत छै.

एहि विनाशकारी घटनाक एहि मद्देनजर नेपाल आ चीनक बीच सीमा पारक बेहतर समन्वय हमरा लोकनि पहिने सँ देखि रहल छी । उच्च प्राथमिकता वाला जानकारी साझा करलऽ जाय रहलऽ छै आरू चीनी आरू नेपाली अधिकारियऽ के बीच संचार केरऽ नया चैनल खुल॑ लगलऽ छै — ई आशाजनक, अगर समय सीमा स॑ भी होय गेलऽ छै त॑ बदलाव । कई तरह के लोगऽ न॑ अधिक औपचारिक समन्वय आरू सीमा पार निगरानी नेटवर्क के स्थापना के आह्वान करल॑ छै ।

स्पष्ट कहै लेली कि कोय भी — नेपाल नै, चीन नै, अंतर्राष्ट्रीय वैज्ञानिक समुदाय नै — ई आपदा के शुरुआत करै वाला सूक्ष्म परिवर्तन आरू विशिष्ट जोखिम के पहचान नै करी सकै छेलै । फोरेंसिक विश्लेषण स॑ नया-नया अंतर्दृष्टि मिल॑ लगलऽ छै जेकरऽ उपयोग हम्मं॑ भविष्य म॑ भी ऐसनऽ जोखिम के खोज करै लेली करी सकै छियै, लेकिन ई घटना के शुरुआत अचानक एगो जन आंदोलन स॑ होलै जे बहुत तेजी स॑ चरम प्रवाह म॑ बदली गेलै जेकरा स॑ एक सच्चा अलर्ट साझा नै करलऽ जाब॑ सक॑ । आशा छै कि ई आपदा वू तरह के निरंतर, सीमा पार स॑ निगरानी आरू सहयोग के उत्प्रेरक बनतै जेकरऽ जरूरत ई क्षेत्र क॑ सालौ स॑ छै ।

title: Two trapped workers are pulled alive from Nepal tunnel more than a week after deadly floods - NBC News
description: Two trapped workers are pulled alive from Nepal tunnel more than a week after deadly floods  NBC News9 Days After Flood, Two Men Are Pulled Alive From Mud-Filled Tunnels in Nepal  The New York TimesTwo men pulled alive from Nepal hydropower plant tunnel nine days after floods  CNN
publisher.title: NBC News
full_article:
POKHARA, Nepal — Two workers in Nepal were pulled out alive from a hydropower tunnel Friday, nine days after devastating floods swept the Himalayan region and left thousands of people dead or missing.

In a rare glimmer of hope, emergency teams rescued two men — a mechanical foreman named Sanjay Sah, 30, and a mechanical supervisor named Kabir Maharjan, 45, according to Nepal’s army and the country’s National Disaster Risk Reduction & Management Authority. A body was also recovered, Nepal’s army said.

00:33 Two Nepal flood survivors rescued from hydropower tunnel 00:00 00:00

Rescue officials said the voices of other workers could be heard inside the tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydropower plant along the Trishuli River in Nepal’s border district of Rasuwa. At least 557 workers are still believed to be missing there, with about 115 believed to be trapped in the main tunnel, according to the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal.

In a video shared by Nepalese authorities, Sah said he spent his days trapped underground “chanting mantras to give myself hope” while hearing others trapped and calling out for help.

Sah said the “primary duty” of his job is “to safeguard everyone’s life,” adding that there were some 40 to 50 people in the tunnel at the time of the incident.

“I made sure to evacuate everyone else, but I didn’t get the chance to escape myself,” he said, speaking from the hospital in the video.

He said there could still be other survivors on his side of the tunnel, while there could be workers on the powerhouse side of the tunnel “who didn’t make it out in time.”

Nepal’s army released images of the dramatic rescue on its official Facebook page, including one showing the first rescued worker covered in mud and being carried from the site on a rescuer’s shoulder.

“When hope is alive, even the impossible becomes possible,” the image caption read.

The rescue operation at the Trishuli 3A hydropower project Friday. Nepali Army

Officials said both men were flown to a hospital in Kathmandu, the capital, for treatment.

“I can’t explain what we are feeling at the moment. We are just grateful to God,” Amir Maharjan, the brother of one of the rescued workers, told The Associated Press. He said the family was on its way to the hospital to see him.

The large-scale operation has involved 75 army personnel, 18 police officers and multiple experts, the army said.

Army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet said one of the survivors told rescuers that more people were still alive inside the tunnel.

“We are waiting for the rescue of more and more people,” Communication Minister Bikram Timilsina wrote on his Facebook page.

More than 900 workers are missing from about a dozen hydropower projects in Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels, according to local officials.

Rescuers have been struggling to access the hydropower projects, many of which are in remote, mountainous areas, with bad weather adding to the difficulties. The flooding damaged roads and collapsed sections of tunnels, filling them with mud and other debris and blocking some entrances.

Aided by foreign experts, rescue teams have been working around the clock using controlled blasts, excavators and earth-moving equipment to try to reach the trapped workers amid concerns about air quality in the tunnels and the workers’ access to drinking water.

Nepal’s army said Friday that a separate rescue effort had recovered two bodies from a tunnel at the Langtang Hydropower Project.

Rescuers first heard voices from inside the tunnel Friday morning. Nepali Army

Authorities in Nepal say at least 1,294 people were killed and more than 5,000 remain missing after the Aug. 26 disaster, which is believed to have been set off by a high-altitude glacier collapse on the border between Nepal and China’s Tibet region.

Nepal’s disaster agency estimated Friday that flooding caused at least 387.5 billion Nepalese rupees ($2.5 billion) in damage to infrastructure and property.

Nepalese authorities said a national day of mourning will be observed on Sept. 7 in honor of those who lost their lives during the flood. The national flag will be flown at half-staff at government offices and Nepali embassies and missions abroad.

Rescue efforts are also still underway in China, where a mudslide hit a major land crossing between the two countries, with the only road to the site in Tibet’s Gyirong county fully reopening only Wednesday. Chinese officials say at least 31 people were killed and 531 are missing on the Tibet side of the border.

More than 800 foreign nationals are among those missing in the area, which is popular with trekkers and pilgrims. According to the State Department, 75 Americans remained unaccounted for as of Wednesday, while 16 had made their way to safety.

बचाव अधिकारी सब कहलनि जे, नेपाल के सीमावर्ती जिला रसुवा के त्रिशुली नदी के कात में बनल त्रिशुली 3ए जलविद्युत संयंत्र में सुरंग के भीतर अन्य मजदूर के आवाज सुनाई देल गेल अछि। ओतय एखनहु कम सँ कम ५५७ मजदूर लापता हेबाक आशंका अछि, जाहि मे लगभग ११५ गोटे मुख्य सुरंग मे फँसल आशंका अछि, नेपालक स्वतन्त्र विद्युत उत्पादक संघ जनौलक अछि ।

नेपाली अधिकारी द्वारा साझा कएल गेल एकटा वीडियो मे साह कहलनि जे, ओ अपन दिन भूमिगत रूप सँ फँसल “अपना केँ आशा देबाक लेल मंत्रक जाप करैत” बिताबैत छलाह, जखन कि दोसर लोक केँ फँसल सुनैत छलाह आ मददि लेल आवाज दैत छलाह।

साह नँ कहलकै कि हुनकौ काम के “प्राथमिक कर्तव्य” “सब के जान के रक्षा करना” छै, आरू कहलकै कि घटना के समय सुरंग मँ लगभग 40 सँ 50 लोग छेलै ।

वीडियो मे अस्पताल स’ बजैत ओ कहलनि जे, हम बाकी सब गोटे के बाहर निकालब सुनिश्चित केलहुं, मुदा हमरा खुद भागबाक मौका नहि भेटल।

ओ कहलनि जे सुरंग के हुनकर तरफ एखनो आओर बचि गेल लोक भ’ सकैत छथि, जखन कि सुरंग के पावरहाउस कात मे एहन मजदूर भ’ सकैत छथि “जे समय पर बाहर नहि निकलि सकलाह.”

नेपाल केरऽ सेना न॑ अपनऽ आधिकारिक फेसबुक पेज प॑ नाटकीय बचाव केरऽ तस्वीर जारी करलकै, जेकरा म॑ एगो म॑ पहिलऽ बचाव करलऽ गेलऽ मजदूर क॑ थाल म॑ ढंकलऽ आरू बचावकर्ता केरऽ कंधा प॑ साइट स॑ ल॑ जायलऽ जाय रहलऽ छै ।

छवि कैप्शन मे लिखल छल जे जखन आशा जीवित रहैत अछि तखन असंभव सेहो संभव भ जाइत अछि।

त्रिशुली 3ए जलविद्युत परियोजना मे शुक्रदिन बचाव अभियान। नेपाली सेना

अधिकारी सब कहलनि जे, दुनू गोटे के इलाज के लेल राजधानी काठमांडू के अस्पताल पहुंचाओल गेल।

बचावल गेल एकटा मजदूर के भाई अमीर महर्जन द एसोसिएटेड प्रेस के कहलनि जे, हम ई नहि बता सकैत छी जे एखन हमरा सब के की महसूस भ रहल अछि, हम सब बस भगवान के आभारी छी। ओ कहलनि जे, परिवार हुनका देखय लेल अस्पताल जा रहल छल।

सेना के कहब अछि जे पैघ पैमाना पर भेल एहि अभियान मे सेना के 75 जवान, 18 पुलिस अधिकारी आ कईटा विशेषज्ञ शामिल भेल अछि।

सेना प्रवक्ता ब्रिगेडियर एस. जनरल राजा राम बस्नेट कहलनि जे, बचि गेल एकटा लोक बचावकर्ता के कहलनि जे, सुरंग के अंदर एखनो आओर लोक जीवित अछि।

संचार मंत्री बिक्रम तिमिलसिना अपन फेसबुक पेज पर लिखलनि जे, हम सब बेसी स बेसी लोक के बचाव के इंतजार क रहल छी।

नेपालमे लगभग एक दर्जन जलविद्युत परियोजनासँ ९००सँ बेसी मजदूर लापता अछि, जाहिमे लगभग ५०० गोटे सुरंगमे फँसल मानल जा रहल अछि स्थानीय अधिकारीसभक अनुसार ।

बचावकर्मी क॑ जलविद्युत परियोजना तलक पहुँचै म॑ परेशानी होय रहलऽ छै, जेकरा म॑ स॑ बहुत सारा दूरस्थ, पहाड़ी इलाका म॑ छै, जेकरा चलतें खराब मौसम न॑ दिक्कत क॑ बढ़ाबै छै । बाढ़ि स सड़क क्षतिग्रस्त भ गेल आ सुरंग क किछु हिस्सा खसि पड़ल, जाहि स थाल आ अन्य मलबा भरि गेल आ किछु प्रवेश द्वार बंद भ गेल।

सुरंगऽ म॑ हवा के गुणवत्ता आरू मजदूरऽ के पेयजल के पहुँच के चिंता के बीच विदेशी विशेषज्ञऽ के सहायता स॑ बचाव टीम न॑ नियंत्रित विस्फोट, खुदाई आरू मिट्टी क॑ चलै वाला उपकरण के इस्तेमाल करी क॑ चौबीसों घंटा काम करी क॑ फंसलऽ मजदूरऽ तलक पहुँचै के कोशिश करी रहलऽ छै ।

नेपालक सेना शुक्रदिन कहलनि जे, अलग-अलग बचाव प्रयास मे लंगटांग जलविद्युत परियोजनाक सुरंग सँ दू टा लाश बरामद कयल गेल अछि।

बचावकर्मी सबस पहिने शुक्रदिन भोर मे सुरंग क अंदर स आवाज सुनलक। नेपाली सेना

नेपाल केरऽ अधिकारियऽ के कहना छै कि २६ अगस्त केरऽ आपदा के बाद कम स॑ कम १,२९४ लोगऽ के मौत होय गेलऽ छै आरू ५,००० स॑ भी अधिक लोग लापता छै, जेकरऽ शुरुआत नेपाल आरू चीन केरऽ तिब्बत क्षेत्र के सीमा प॑ उच्च ऊँचाई प॑ ग्लेशियर के गिरला के कारण मानलऽ जाय रहलऽ छै ।

नेपाल केरऽ आपदा एजेंसी न॑ शुक्रवार क॑ अनुमान लगैलकै कि बाढ़ स॑ कम स॑ कम ३८७.५ अरब नेपाली रुपया (२.५ अरब डॉलर) के नुकसान पहुँचलै ।

नेपाली अधिकारि सब बाढिक समयमे जान गंवा देनिहारके सम्मानमे ७ सितम्बरके राष्ट्रिय शोक दिवस मनाओल जाएत बतौलनि । सरकारी कार्यालय आ विदेशमे रहल नेपाली दूतावास आ मिशनमे आधा कर्मचारीमे राष्ट्रिय झंडा फहराओल जाएत ।

चीन म॑ भी बचाव के प्रयास अखनी भी जारी छै, जहां दूनू देशऽ के बीच एगो बड़ऽ लैंड क्रॉसिंग प॑ कीचड़ गिरी गेलऽ छै, आरू तिब्बत केरऽ ग्योरोंग काउंटी म॑ ई जगह प॑ जाय वाला एकमात्र सड़क बुधवार क॑ ही पूरा तरह स॑ खुललऽ छै । चीनी अधिकारी के कहनाय छनि जे सीमा के तिब्बत कात कम सं कम 31 लोक के मौत भ गेल अछि आओर 531 लोक लापता अछि.

ट्रेकर्स आ तीर्थयात्री के बीच लोकप्रिय एहि इलाका मे लापता लोक मे 800 सं बेसि विदेशी नागरिक सेहो शामिल छथिन्ह. विदेश विभाग के अनुसार बुधदिन तक 75 अमेरिकी के हिसाब-किताब नहिं अछि, जखन कि 16 गोटे सुरक्षित स्थान पर पहुंच गेल छलाह.

title: ‘They’ll be finding bodies next year’: a renowned forensic scientist on Nepal’s ‘extreme challenges’ - The Guardian

full_article:
The bodies of some of those killed in the Nepal-Tibet flood disaster may never be found, and some of those that are may never be identified, a world-renowned forensic scientist says.

Prof Richard Bassed, the head of forensic medicine at Melbourne’s Monash University, spent three months in Thailand after the 2004 Boxing Day tsunami and also helped to identify victims of Victoria’s catastrophic Black Saturday bushfires in 2009.

Now he has watched as authorities in Nepal and Tibet struggle to find and identify the dead amid the agonies of the living after last week’s devastating flash flood. More than 1,250 people have been confirmed dead, with more than 5,000 missing.

Prakrit has already lost her father. As Nepal’s morgues fill, she hopes her DNA can be used to find her mother Read more

The difficult terrain, and inadequate communications and resources, would all hamper efforts, Bassed says.

“They could be washed anywhere, buried under mud. I imagine there’s a number they’ll never find. I imagine they’ll be finding bodies next year.”

Authorities are still finding bodies from the 2011 Japanese tsunami, he says.

The bodies from the 2004 tsunami were relatively easy to recover, but it still took a year to identify 5,000 people, he says.

“And there were still some we couldn’t identify.”

Asked how he copes with the horror of death on such a scale, he says he has “never found it long-term traumatising”.

“Occasionally you’ll see something that’ll hit close to home. For me, it’s kids,” he says.

“And the randomness. The randomness of a tsunami, the randomness of this massive flood. That gets to you.

“But mostly you have your clinical face on, you do the best you can and know you’re doing it to help people.”

Authorities will use rapidly improving DNA techniques to try to identify the victims. This week Nepali police urged relatives of missing tourists to provide “a fresh blood sample for DNA profiling and two passport-sized photographs” to the pathology laboratory at the police hospital in Kathmandu.

But authorities in Nepal and Tibet face “extreme challenges”, Bassed says.

They include the danger of more mudslides, the complexity of co-ordinating across international borders and the likelihood of local mortuaries and other infrastructure being overwhelmed by the number of bodies.

The mix of nations and religions also brings issues of different cultural beliefs around how and whether people should be buried.

The International Committee of the Red Cross and other international bodies have published Management of dead bodies after disasters: A field manual for First Responders to help people deal with bodies in a “proper and dignified way”, including by taking down details that will later help experts identify the remains.

First responders – often locals who are not forensic experts – are trained to follow those guidelines, tagging bodies in the hope they will later be matched to a missing person.

They give each body a unique code (for example the name of the place, the name of the team and a number). They will also take photos of the body and any distinguishing features such as gold teeth, clothing and tattoos, including that code in the image.

View image in fullscreen ‘You have your clinical face on, you do the best you can’ … Prof Richard Bassed. Photograph: John Lloyd Fillingham / Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine

Then they place the body in a body bag and organise its “orderly temporary storage”, again marked with the body code.

In Nepal, morgues are filling up and mass burials are taking place, as authorities collect DNA samples.

Bassed says most of the missing Australians would have dental records, which could help to identify them, but in Nepal many matches will be made using DNA or pictures, as fingerprints will often no longer be usable.

Work is under way to use AI and facial recognition technology to identify victims after disasters, but it’s controversial – Ukraine used Clearview AI software after the Russian invasion in 2022, just as the company was fined millions of dollars for collecting images of people in the UK and elsewhere without consent. Widespread use is also limited by access to the technology.

Bassed says researchers have also worked to devise an algorithm that could use passport or driver’s licence photos to identify someone.

“But it’s really complex, and it depends how they look, the trauma,” he says.

Another possibility is CT scanning, which can get a serial number from joint replacements, for example.

“But trying to get this technology to the places it’s needed in the middle of a disaster … you need running water, you need electricity … you could put CT scanners into helicopters, but all this costs an awful lot of money.”

नेपाल-तिब्बत बाढ़ि आपदा मे मारल गेल किछु लोकक शव कहियो नहि भेटि सकैत अछि, आ जे किछु अछि ओकर पहचान कहियो नहि भ सकैत अछि, विश्व प्रसिद्ध फोरेंसिक वैज्ञानिक कहैत छथि ।

मेलबर्न केरऽ मोनाश विश्वविद्यालय केरऽ फोरेंसिक मेडिसिन केरऽ प्रमुख प्रो रिचर्ड बेस्ड न॑ २००४ केरऽ बॉक्सिंग डे केरऽ सुनामी के बाद तीन महीना थाईलैंड म॑ बिताबै के काम करलकै आरू २००९ म॑ विक्टोरिया म॑ ब्लैक सैटरडे केरऽ भयावह झाड़ी म॑ आग लगला के शिकार लोगऽ के पहचान करै म॑ भी मदद करलकै ।

आब ओ देखैत रहलाह अछि जे पिछला सप्ताह के विनाशकारी आकस्मिक बाढ़ि के बाद जीवित लोक के पीड़ा के बीच नेपाल आओर तिब्बत के अधिकारी मृतक के खोजय आओर पहचान करय लेल संघर्ष क रहल छथिन्ह. 1250 स बेसी लोक के मौत के पुष्टि भेल अछि, जाहि मे 5000 स बेसी लोक लापता अछि।

प्राकृत अपन पिताकेँ गमा चुकल अछि । जेना-जेना नेपाल के मुर्दाघर भरैत जाइत अछि, हुनका उम्मीद अछि जे हुनकर डीएनए के इस्तेमाल सं हुनकर मां के खोजल जा सकैत अछि आओर पढ़ू

बास्सेड के कहना छै कि कठिन इलाका, आरू अपर्याप्त संचार आरू संसाधन, सब प्रयास म॑ बाधा पहुँचतै ।

“ओ सभ कतहु धोल जा सकैत छल, थाल-कादो मे गाड़ल जा सकैत छल. हम कल्पना करैत छी जे एकटा नंबर छैक जे ओकरा सभ केँ कहियो नहि भेटतैक. हम कल्पना करैत छी जे अगिला साल ओकरा सभ केँ लाश भेटतैक.”

हुनकऽ कहना छै कि अधिकारियऽ क॑ अखनी भी २०११ केरऽ जापानी सुनामी केरऽ लाश मिल॑ लगलऽ छै ।

हुनकऽ कहना छै कि २००४ केरऽ सुनामी केरऽ लाश क॑ बरामद करना अपेक्षाकृत आसान छेलै, लेकिन तभियो ५,००० लोगऽ के पहचान करै म॑ एक साल लगलै ।

“आ एखनो किछु एहन छल जकरा हम सभ चिन्हित नहि क’ सकलहुँ.”

ब्रेकिंग न्यूज ऑस्ट्रेलिया ईमेल के लेल साइन अप करू

ई पूछला प॑ कि हुनी ऐसनऽ पैमाना प॑ मौत केरऽ भयावहता स॑ कोना निपटै छै, हुनी कहै छै कि हुनका “कहियो ई दीर्घकालिक आघातकारी नै लगलै” ।

ओ कहैत छथि, "कखनो काल किछु एहन देखबा मे आओत जे घरक नजदीक मे टक्कर मारत, हमरा लेल त’ बच्चा सभ अछि।"

“आ बेतरतीबता।सुनामीक बेतरतीबता, एहि विशाल बाढ़िक बेतरतीबता।से अहाँ धरि पहुँचि जाइत अछि।

“मुदा बेसी काल अहाँक क्लिनिकल चेहरा पर रहैत अछि, अहाँ जतेक नीक काज क’ सकैत छी से करैत छी आ जनैत छी जे अहाँ ई काज लोकक मददि लेल क’ रहल छी.”

अधिकारियऽ न॑ तेजी स॑ सुधारत॑ डीएनए तकनीक के इस्तेमाल करी क॑ पीड़ितऽ के पहचान करै के कोशिश करतै । एहि सप्ताह नेपाली पुलिस लापता पर्यटक के परिजन स आग्रह केलक अछि जे काठमांडू के पुलिस अस्पताल के पैथोलॉजी प्रयोगशाला में “डीएनए प्रोफाइलिंग के लेल एकटा ताजा खून के नमूना आ दू टा पासपोर्ट साइज के फोटो” उपलब्ध कराबी।

title: ‘Everyone seems to have forgotten’: In Tibet, flood-hit families search for the missing and grapple with China’s silence - The Guardian
description: ‘Everyone seems to have forgotten’: In Tibet, flood-hit families search for the missing and grapple with China’s silence  The Guardian
publisher.title: The Guardian
full_article:
F an Hong last heard from her husband on the morning of the Nepal-Tibet disaster. More than a week later, the 31-year-old is desperately searching for information about Lin Bo, who was working on a Chinese highway project in Nepal. Struggling to get information from authorities, Fan turned to social media for help.

“My husband works on a project in Nepal, about 5 kilometres from the Gyirong border crossing. I want to know what the situation is, but I haven’t been able to reach him,” the 31-year-old from China’s Sichuan province wrote on Rednote.

Her post has gained more than 18,000 likes and nearly 4,600 comments. She is one of many in China with missing loved ones trying to piece together information they are finding online, as Tibetan advocate groups say information is being suppressed on that side of the border.

View image in fullscreen A screen outside a shopping mall in Beijing shows a news report featuring rescue workers at in Gyirong county. Photograph: Greg Baker/AFP/Getty Images

Lin began working on repairing the Syaphrubesi-Rasuwagadhi Highway – which links Nepal to Tibet, China, through the Gyirong border crossing – in 2024. He had been living on site and working on a 16km stretch of the road.

Fan says that rescue missions into the construction site have stalled. She says relatives of survivors are asking the Chinese authorities for permission to send up their own drones or helicopters to look for the missing.

“I feel more disheartened with each passing day. Feel colder and colder inside,” she told the Guardian. “I don’t even have any tears left.”

It is just over a week since the collapse of a glacier triggered devastating floods along the Nepal-Tibet border, destroying entire villages and killing more than 1,200 people. On Wednesday, 4,216 remained missing, according to Nepal officials. Chinese authorities say 541 remain unaccounted for on the Tibetan side, including 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries.

The relatively low official death toll from the Chinese authorities has also raised some concern among Tibetan advocacy groups, given the scale of the destruction seen in video footage. “All we can do is imagine – and that should terrify us,” said Tenzin Choekyi from Tibet Watch. As of Thursday, China had officially reported 21 people killed.

While in China, the official narrative heavily focuses on rescue efforts, online posts across Chinese social media show an emotional outpouring of grief and mourning. On Douyin, China’s version of TikTok, photographs of missing border inspection officers are shared under the hashtag “Salute to heroes guarding the nation’s gateway”.

In China, families with missing loved ones say they are relying on information from Nepal, as well as foreign embassies and social media. Tibetan advocate groups say information on the Tibetan side of the border remains heavily restricted.

On 30 August, Tibetan police reported that 10 people had been punished for spreading what authorities called “false information” about the scale of the disaster online.

“This crackdown is obstructing not just public reporting of the disaster and relief efforts but the basic work of establishing whether communities are alive and receiving the support that they need,” said Tencho Gyatso, president of the US-based Tibetan advocacy group the International Campaign for Tibet (ICT)

“Sources are now afraid to speak to outside groups including ICT. One source told ICT it was “extremely unsafe” to speak. Another asked us not to make further contact given the potential ramifications,” she said.

View image in fullscreen A press conference held Gyirong after the Nepal-Tibet disaster. Photograph: China News Service/Getty Images

Fan says she is mainly relying on information from Nepal.

“Everyone seems to have forgotten about the workers on the Syaphrubesi–Rasuwagadhi Highway project … All the news coverage is about the hydropower station [in Nepal].

Families of foreign tourists who went missing in Tibet are also desperately searching for information,

View image in fullscreen Sridhar Avvari. Photograph: Supplied

British nationals Sridhar Avvari, 43, his wife, Deepti, 41, and their 14-year-old son Abhinav went missing near the immigration area at Gyirong on 26 August, close to the Nepal-Tibet border. The family lives in India and relatives believe they over on to the Tibetan side.

In a call to the family days earlier, Deepti Avvari told them that there would be no signal but would talk when she returned to an area with network activity. After the flash flood, calls to Deepti’s phone stopped connecting.

“There was no signal, so we can’t talk … After coming down, I will call you again,” Deepti told Priyanka Rapaka, her sister in law.

They are desperately waiting for updates.

View image in fullscreen Deepti Avvari is among the missing. Photograph: Supplied

“We didn’t get any information from China … We are checking online only who are rescued and … how many are dead,” Rapaka said.

View image in fullscreen British national Neetu Goyal Tiwari. Photograph: Supplied

Chinese authorities say they are now able to reach the main disaster zone by road. According to state media they are describing the region as an active search and rescue operation and are searching for hundreds of missing people.

Naresh Goyal is anxiously waiting for news about his sister, Neetu Goyal Tiwari, a 51-year-old missing British national who flew from India to Kathmandu on 14 August to join an Isha Foundation pilgrimage.

“The last message received is that they have reached Gyirong immigration office. “They said they are going to check out.” He says he found his sister’s name on a list of missing people circulating on social media, but said he is unsure where the list originated. Getting information out of the Chinese authorities has been difficult.

“Whenever we ask the China government, they are telling us that they will update us through the embassy of the UK,” he says.

“It is very painful here Now we have spent at least seven days and every minute we are waiting,” Goyal says.

title: Nepal Tunnel Rescue Offers Hope for 5,000 Missing as Operation Blessing Aids Flood Victims - cbn.com
description: Nepal Tunnel Rescue Offers Hope for 5,000 Missing as Operation Blessing Aids Flood Victims  cbn.com
publisher.title: cbn.com
full_article:
In the aftermath of the disaster in Nepal, two hydropower workers have been found alive in a tunnel more than a week after the flooding. Crews continue to search for other workers who may have survived in air pockets inside the mud-filled tunnels.

The discovery is raising hopes of reaching dozens of others believed to still be trapped, nine days after deadly flash floods swept away villages and buried parts of the Himalayan region in mud and debris.

Approximately 5,000 people are still missing, and the death toll continues to climb. It is now nearing 1,300.

The U.N.'s humanitarian agency says access to the region remains the biggest challenge, with more than 40 bridges destroyed.

CBN's Operation Blessing is in Nepal, helping bring aid to victims. This week, the team joined local partners to assemble and distribute hygiene kits for families affected by the disaster.

Operation Blessing is on the scene to help the Nepali community. Click here to support Operation Blessing's efforts.

The kits include essential items such as soap, wet wipes, sanitary pads, toothbrushes, and solar lamps.

Team members also traveled to a children's shelter, where they delivered fruit, milk, and other essential supplies. They then visited a local church and distributed hygiene kits and solar lamps to help families in need.

Operation Blessing's Diego Traverso said, "Remember, these families, they lost everything. Everything. They have no clothes, no home. They have no means to survive, and Operation Blessing is stepping up to support them, to meet them where the need is. Right now, they need food, they need water, they need hygiene kits..."

Operation Blessing India is working to send a medical team to Nepal in the coming days.

title: Flooding in Nepal: What You Need to Know - International Medical Corps
description: Flooding in Nepal: What You Need to Know  International Medical Corps
publisher.title: International Medical Corps
full_article:
To find out more about our response, please visit our Nepal alert page.

On the morning of August 26, a glacial collapse near the Nepal–China border sent powerful flash floods and mudslides along a 72-kilometer stretch of the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers in Nepal, devastating dozens of villages and sweeping away homes, roads, bridges and power plants. At least 1,250 people have been confirmed dead, while thousands remain missing—numbers that are likely to go up as search-and-recovery operations continue.

The impact of the collapse was so strong that it triggered a 5.2-magnitude tremor. Later analysis revealed that the tremor was not an earthquake, but was in fact seismic energy generated by the collapse of glacial rock and ice, followed by debris flow.

Workers use bulldozers to rebuild the roads following flash floods at Devighat in Bidur municipality, Nuwakot district.

Why Were the Floods So Devastating?

The glacier collapse triggered a chain reaction of events. When the large chunk of ice crashed into the river valley below, it pushed huge amounts of water, ice, mud and rocks into the river, creating a massive and powerful surge that moved downhill rapidly, carrying with it sediment, boulders and trees. As the flood traveled downstream through Nepal, it swept away everything in its path—people, homes, roads, bridges and more.

Which Are the Worst-hit Areas?

The water surge destroyed the Gyirong checkpoint at the Nepal-China border. As the waters rushed downstream, many districts in central Nepal—including Chitwan, Dhading, Nuwakot and Rasuwa—were affected. Rasuwa, with several hydropower projects and a population of about 50,000, was the hardest hit.

Floods in Nepal: 1980–2026

Nepal has witnessed many floods since the 1980s, mainly due to heavy monsoon rains and landslides. The Bhote Koshi-Trishuli flood of August 2026 is one of the country’s deadliest in recent decades. Here’s a list of some of the other devastating floods in Nepal:

Year What Happened 1989 Relentless monsoon rain caused widespread flooding, killing at least 700 people. 1993 Monsoon floods and landslides killed more than 1,300 people and affected more than 85,000 families. 2002 Floods and landslides claimed more than 400 lives and affected nearly 40,000 families. 2024 Heavy monsoon rainfall triggered floods and landslides across the country, killing more than 200 people. 2026 Powerful flash floods swept through the Nepal–China border, rushing downstream through Nepal’s Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers. At least 1,250 people have died and thousands remain missing.

What Is the Extent of Damage from the Current Flood?

The floods have caused extensive damage to roads, bridges, homes and power infrastructure, complicating relief and rescue work as humanitarian responders struggle to reach cut-off communities. Nepali authorities estimate that about 20,000 houses in flood-affected areas will need rebuilding. Many of the houses that were left standing are no longer habitable, as they’re filled with mud and debris.

What Are the Urgent Humanitarian Needs?

Thousands of flood-affected people have lost their homes and livelihoods. They urgently need medicines, medical supplies, food, clean water and hygiene materials, as well as psychosocial support.

Has International Medical Corps Responded in Nepal Before?

Yes. We were one of the first humanitarian organizations to respond in Nepal following a deadly 7.8-magnitude earthquake in April 2015. Our Emergency Response Team deployed mobile medical units to some of the hardest-hit locations, providing lifesaving medical care within 48 hours of the disaster. Our teams worked closely with local and international partners to provide medical treatment and supplies, as well as other emergency services, to those affected.

MD Michael Karch and a team of local villagers had to climb some 3,000 feet to Laprak, to evacuate Madhira Singh to the Gorkha District Hospital. Singh had been trapped under his home for two days and without medical attention for nine days after the earthquake in April 2015.

What is International Medical Corps Doing to Help Now?

We are leveraging established relationships in the country to respond through a network of trusted local partners already operating in the affected areas, to provide essential health services for affected populations in displacement shelters and in affected communities. We will also be supporting the distribution of critical relief supplies—including food, shelter materials and hygiene items—to help families meet their most urgent needs.

ग्लेशियर केरऽ गिरला स॑ घटना के श्रृंखलाबद्ध प्रतिक्रिया शुरू होय गेलै । जखन बर्फक पैघ टुकड़ा नीचाँ नदीक घाटी मे खसि पड़ल तऽ भारी मात्रा मे पानि, बर्फ, थाल आ चट्टान केँ नदी मे धकेलि देलक, जाहि सँ एकटा विशाल आ शक्तिशाली उफान उत्पन्न भेल जे तेजी सँ नीचाँ दिस बढ़ैत गेल, अपन संग तलछट, बोल्डर आ गाछ-बिरिछ ल' गेल. जेना-जेना बाढ़ि नेपाल होइत नीचाँ दिस जाइत छल, अपन बाट मे जे किछु छल-लोक, घर, सड़क, पुल आओर बहुत किछु बहरा गेल।

कोन-कोन क्षेत्र सबसँ बेसी प्रभावित अछि ?

पानिक उफानसँ नेपाल-चीन सीमापर ग्यरोंग नाका नष्ट भऽ गेल अछि । जेना-जेना पानि नीचाँ दिस दौड़ैत गेल, मध्य नेपालक बहुतो जिला-जाहि मे चितवन, धादिङ, नुवाकोट आ रसुवा-सहित अछि- प्रभावित भेल । कईटा जलविद्युत परियोजना आ करीब 50 हजार क आबादी वाला रसुवा कए सबस बेसी नुकसान भेल।

नेपालमे बाढ़ि : १९८०–२०२६

नेपाल मे 1980 के दशक स बहुत रास बाढ़ि आयल अछि, जेकर मुख्य कारण अछि भारी मानसून बरखा आ भूस्खलन। अगस्त 2026 केरऽ भोटे कोशी-त्रिशुली बाढ़ देश केरऽ हाल केरऽ दशकऽ म॑ सबसें जानलेवा बाढ़ऽ म॑ स॑ एक छै । नेपालक किछु अन्य विनाशकारी बाढ़िक सूची प्रस्तुत अछि :

वर्ष की भेल 1989 अथक मानसून बरखा के कारण व्यापक बाढ़ि आबि गेल छल, जाहि मे कम सं कम 700 लोक के मौत भ गेल छल. १९९३ मानसून के बाढ़ि आ भूस्खलन मे १३०० सँ बेसी लोकक मृत्यु भेल आ ८५ हजार सँ बेसी परिवार प्रभावित भेल । 2002 बाढ़ि आ भूस्खलन मे 400 सं बेसी लोकक जान गेल आ लगभग 40,000 परिवार प्रभावित भेल. 2024 मानसून केरऽ भारी बारिश के वजह स॑ देश भर म॑ बाढ़ आरू भूस्खलन होय ​​गेलै, जेकरा म॑ २०० स॑ भी अधिक लोगऽ के मौत होय गेलै । 2026 नेपाल–चीन सीमा पर शक्तिशाली आकस्मिक बाढ़ि नेपालक भोटे कोशी आ त्रिशुली नदीक माध्यमे नीचाँ दौड़ल । कम सं कम 1250 लोक के मौत भ गेल अछि आओर हजारों लोक लापता अछि.

वर्तमान बाढ़ि स क्षति के सीमा की अछि ?

बाढ़ि के कारण सड़क, पुल, घर आ बिजली के बुनियादी ढाँचा के व्यापक नुकसान भेल अछि, जाहि सं राहत आ बचाव के काज जटिल भ गेल अछि, कियाकि मानवीय प्रतिक्रियाकर्ता कट ऑफ समुदाय तक पहुंचय लेल संघर्ष क रहल अछि. नेपाली अधिकारीक अनुमान अछि जे बाढ़ि प्रभावित इलाका मे करीब 20 हजार मकान के पुनर्निर्माण के जरूरत पड़त। जे घर ठाढ़ रहि गेल छल, ओहि मे सँ बहुतो घर आब रहबाक योग्य नहि अछि, कारण ओ सभ थाल-कादो आ मलबा सँ भरल अछि.

तत्काल मानवीय आवश्यकता की अछि ?

हजारों बाढ़ि प्रभावित लोक के घर-घर आओर रोजी-रोटी के नुकसान भ गेल अछि. हुनका दवाई, चिकित्सा आपूर्ति, भोजन, स्वच्छ पानी आ स्वच्छता सामग्री कें संग-संग मनोसामाजिक सहायता कें तत्काल जरूरत छै.

नेपाल मे अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय चिकित्सा कोर पहिने प्रतिक्रिया देने छल कि नहि ?

हँ। अप्रैल २०१५ म॑ ७.८ तीव्रता के घातक भूकंप के बाद नेपाल म॑ प्रतिक्रिया दै वाला पहलऽ मानवीय संगठनऽ म॑ स॑ एक छेलियै ।हमरऽ आपातकालीन प्रतिक्रिया दल न॑ कुछ सबसें बेसी प्रभावित स्थानऽ प॑ मोबाइल मेडिकल यूनिट तैनात करी क॑ आपदा के ४८ घंटा के भीतर जीवन रक्षक चिकित्सा सेवा उपलब्ध कराय देलकै । हमरऽ टीम न॑ स्थानीय आरू अंतर्राष्ट्रीय भागीदारऽ के साथ मिलक॑ प्रभावित लोगऽ क॑ चिकित्सा उपचार आरू आपूर्ति के साथ-साथ अन्य आपातकालीन सेवा भी उपलब्ध करैलकै ।

एमडी माइकल कर्च आ स्थानीय ग्रामीण के टीम के करीब 3000 फीट चढ़ि क लप्राक पहुंचय पड़ल, जाहि सं मधीरा सिंह के गोरखा जिला अस्पताल पहुंचाओल जा सकय. सिंह अप्रैल 2015 मे आयल भूकंप के बाद दू दिन सं घर के नीचा फंसल छलाह आओर नौ दिन सं बिना कोनो चिकित्सा के देखभाल केने छलाह.

इंटरनेशनल मेडिकल कोर आब मदद करय लेल की क रहल अछि?

हम देश मे स्थापित संबंधक कें लाभ उठा रहल छी जे प्रभावित क्षेत्रक मे पइहले सं संचालित भरोसेमंद स्थानीय भागीदारक कें नेटवर्क कें माध्यम सं जवाब दे रहल छै, विस्थापन आश्रय स्थल आ प्रभावित समुदायक मे प्रभावित आबादी कें लेल आवश्यक स्वास्थ्य सेवाक प्रदान करय कें लेल. हम महत्वपूर्ण राहत आपूर्ति कें वितरण कें सेहो समर्थन करबय-जइ मे भोजन, आवास सामग्री आ स्वच्छता कें सामान शामिल छै-जइ मे परिवारक कें ओकर सब सं जरूरी जरूरतक कें पूरा करय मे मदद मिल सकय.

नेपाल मे हमर राहत कार्य मे सहयोग करू।

title: Hopes dim for Woodland couple missing in Nepal flooding - Daily Democrat
description: Hopes dim for Woodland couple missing in Nepal flooding  Daily Democrat
publisher.title: Daily Democrat
full_article:
Family members continue to hold out hope for a Woodland couple who remain among the missing in Nepal after catastrophic flooding caused by a glacier collapse.

Hanumantha Rao Unnava and Vasundhara Unnava are among hundreds reported missing as a result of the flash floods along the Nepal-China border on Aug. 26.

Rao had retired from UC Davis in July 2025, where he served as dean of the Graduate School of Management. Vasundhara is a former lecturer at the university.

The couple are Woodland residents and had embarked on a retirement trip that was to include a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, followed by two months in India with family. Rao is 66 years old.

At least 1,287 people were killed in the Aug. 26 floods, likely caused by a glacier collapse, and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to the country’s disaster management agency. China said late Wednesday that 21 people were killed and 541 were missing on the Tibet side of the border.

Nepal’s disaster agency estimated Friday that flooding caused at least $2.5 billion in damage to infrastructure and property.

Thursday, UC Davis Chancellor and Provost Gary May and Mary Croughan issued a statement on behalf of the university directed to family and friends of the Unnavas, who were called “two beloved members of the UC Davis community.”

“We understand they were staying in a hotel in Timure, Nepal, a few kilometers from the border of Nepal and Tibet, when the flash floods occurred on August 26,” the statement reads in part. “They have not been located or heard from since then.

“They have touched countless through their work at the Graduate School of Management and throughout their careers in higher education,” the statement continues. “We are grateful to both Rao and Vasu for their contributions that extend far beyond GSM and UC Davis.”

The Unnavas’ children and extended family are reportedly “pursuing every available avenue to obtain information and requested assistance from U.S. government agencies.

“We continue to hope Rao and Vasu will be found safe and sound. Again, please keep them, their children, and extended family in your thoughts and prayers.”

A group called Indian-American Community News reported the Unnavas were staying at Hotel Kailash in Timure, near the Rasuwagadhi border crossing between Nepal and Tibet. They were traveling with a tour group organized by Himalayan Glacier.

“Their daughter, Vaasavi Unnava, believed her parents had already crossed the border into Tibet when news of the devastating floods emerged,” the publication reported. “She tried reaching them on WhatsApp, expecting the familiar reassurance of a message from her parents. The messages never delivered.”

The publication also reported the couple’s names now appear on an official Nepal Police registry of 65 U.S. citizens reported missing in the disaster.

Both the Unnavas are former Ohio State faculty members who had built long careers at Ohio State’s Fisher College of Business, according to a site titled “All Things Ohio.”

“Rao Unnava earned his doctorate there and spent 32 years at the school as a marketing professor and senior associate dean before becoming dean of the graduate business school at UC Davis,” the publication reported. Vasu Unnava also earned her Ph.D at Fisher and went on to lecture in marketing at UC Davis.”

In a story on Rao’s retirement written by Cindy Brown in July 2025 for UC Davis, he was called a “trailblazer in academia and entrepreneurship.”

“It is thanks to Dean Unnava’s creativity, enthusiasm, and visionary leadership that UC Davis continues to be recognized as one of the most innovative business schools in the country,” said Mary Croughan, provost and executive vice chancellor. “His focus on increasing access to academic programs and elevating the student experience has boosted enrollment, and his collaborative spirit has been such a benefit to UC Davis. I am very grateful that the campus will continue to benefit from Dean Unnava’s ideas, experience, and passion as an esteemed member of our faculty.”

In 2024, Rao was named Dean of the Year by Poets & Quants, an industry publication focused on business education.

“This prestigious award recognized his innovative programming, including expanding opportunities for experiential learning that built skills on the business side of some of UC Davis’s greatest strengths: agriculture, biotechnology, and sustainable energy, among others,” according to Brown’s story. “This year, Poets&Quants named the UC Davis Graduate School of Management among the top 10 business schools to watch in the U.S.

Among Rao’s initiatives, Brown reported, were launching the first online MBA and part-time Master of Management programs in the University of California system, offering credit-bearing stackable credentials that could be applied toward a degree program, deferring tuition for online MBA candidates, creating a lifelong learning platform for the GSM community, and opening all MBA content to alumni for free.

“Under Unnava’s leadership, the Graduate School of Management partnered with UC Davis Athletics to provide student-athletes with a way to continue competing in sports while earning a master’s degree,” Brown wrote. “The collaboration led to an accelerated one-year Master of Management program, and dozens of student-athletes have earned the degree and entered their careers with a solid foundation in business, including accounting, finance, economics, and marketing.”

Following his departure, Rao planned to return to UCD to teach advertising and marketing as a professor in the Graduate School of Management in 2027.

Rao earned a bachelor of science degree in electronics engineering from Jawaharlal Nehru Technological University in Hyderabad, India, a master of business administration degree from the Indian Institute of Management in Calcutta, and a doctorate in business administration from the Fisher College of Business at The Ohio State University.

title: University of Rhode Island water expert from Nepal shares insight into recent flood in South Asian nation | Newswise - Newswise
description: University of Rhode Island water expert from Nepal shares insight into recent flood in South Asian nation | Newswise  Newswise
publisher.title: Newswise
full_article:
A water scientist at the University of Rhode Island, Soni Pradhanang is balancing the professional and the personal, watching her home country of Nepal make news after the recent glacial collapse and flooding there.

As a hydrologist with expertise in environmental geology, flooding, and hazard communication, the events in her home nation are the subject she has made her career in since she left Nepal in 2001. Pradhanang, in URI’s College of the Environment and Life Sciences, conducts research in runoff, flood, drought, and water quality modeling, and has served as a point of contact in URI’s prior work with Nepal. In 2022, during her Fulbright tenure, she served as an instructor for a hydrological modeling training program in Kathmandu, part of a project on “Modeling Hydrological Response to Changes in Climate and Glacier in a Data-Scarce Glacierized Region in Nepal Himalaya.” The training covered core concepts in hydrology, climate change, and cold-region hydrology, providing early-career professionals with the tools to study these issues. “This tragedy highlights the urgent relevance of this research,” she said.

Raised in Kathmandu, approximately 40 miles aerial distance from the affected area in Rasuwa/Langtang National Park, she shares insight into recent events, while keeping tabs on family members and loved ones there.

“For me, this is not an abstract scientific event,” Pradhanang said. “It is a human tragedy affecting communities, families, livelihoods, and landscapes in my home country.”

What were the contributing factors for the recent events in Nepal and has anything like this happened there before?

Based on the best available satellite imagery, seismic observations, and preliminary field interpretation, the disaster in northern Nepal appears to have begun with a rapid failure of a glacierized mountain slope in Langtang National Park near the Nepal–China border. A very large mass of ice, rock, and debris descended into the valley, likely obstructing the Lhende Khola River temporarily. When that unstable blockage failed or was overtopped, it released a powerful debris-laden flood that traveled downstream through the Lhende and Trishuli river valleys.

It is important to be careful about the cause. The collapse itself generated seismic energy comparable to a magnitude 5.2 event; it should not automatically be described as an earthquake-triggered disaster. Scientists worldwide are still determining the relative roles of steep terrain, fractured bedrock, glacier geometry, meltwater, rainfall or snowmelt conditions, and thawing permafrost. Climate warming is a highly relevant background factor because it causes glacier retreat and can thaw the frozen ground that helps stabilize high-mountain rock and ice. But attributing this particular collapse to one single factor would be premature.

Nepal has experienced destructive glacier- and landslide-related floods before, although every event has its own sequence of triggers. Nepal has recorded 26 glacial lake outburst floods since 1977, including events originating both within Nepal and beyond its borders. The Langtang region also has a history of serious mountain hazards, including earthquake-triggered avalanches in 2015 and recent floods and ice-rock avalanches in nearby valleys. This event is especially notable because it appears to involve a rapid ice-and-rock avalanche and a temporary river-dam failure, rather than a conventional moraine-dammed glacial lake suddenly bursting. A similar devastating event occurred in India in 2021, involving a rock-ice avalanche. More recently, in 2024, a cascading glacial lake outburst flood event in Nepal's Thame Valley, triggered by a rock avalanche and a chain reaction of lake breaches, caused widespread destruction. These past disasters highlight the growing danger.

Is there any technology that could provide a warning for an event like this?

No system can predict the exact moment when every slope or glacier will fail, or when a rock-ice avalanche will occur; that would defeat essentially every operational flood warning system in the world. However, technology can provide critical warning—especially once a collapse, blockage, or sudden rise in river level begins.

A strong system would combine satellite monitoring with ground-based instruments. Satellites can detect changes in glacier extent, new or expanding lakes, ground deformation, slope movement, and post-event flood extent. On the ground, river-stage and rainfall gauges, time-lapse cameras, geophones or seismic sensors, and automated alarms can detect rapidly developing hazards. Warnings then need to be distributed immediately via sirens, cell broadcasts, radio, local responders, and community networks.

The limitation is time. In narrow, steep valleys, a debris flood may reach downstream settlements in minutes. Therefore, the system must be automated, resilient to damage, powered and connected with backups, and linked to practiced evacuation plans. Monitoring alone does not save lives unless people receive, understand, trust, and can act on the warning.

What can be done to lessen impact in events like this in the future?

We cannot eliminate all high-mountain hazards, particularly in a country with steep terrain, active geology, and rapidly changing glaciers. But we can substantially reduce loss of life and damage. While predicting these sudden events is incredibly difficult, especially when no immediate rainfall precedes them to trigger traditional flood warnings, several measures can be taken to mitigate the risks and protect vulnerable communities.

The most important actions are to identify hazardous slopes, glaciers, and glacial lakes; map the downstream pathways that floodwaters and debris would follow; install robust monitoring and warning systems; and ensure that communities, schools, hydropower operators, road agencies, and border facilities know exactly how to respond to an alert.

Risk reduction should include four inter-connected elements:

Regular satellite and field monitoring of glacierized slopes, glacial lakes, landslide-prone areas, and thawing permafrost, if any.

Multi-hazard early-warning systems using river-level sensors, cameras, weather stations, seismic instruments, satellite data, and redundant communications.

Community preparedness: alarms, evacuation routes, safe assembly areas, drills, and warning messages that are understandable and accessible to everyone.

Safer planning and infrastructure. Critical facilities such as bridges, hydropower stations, roads, schools, and settlements should, when alternatives exist, be avoided in the highest-hazard flood corridors. Where exposure already exists, structures and evacuation systems should be designed for rapid-onset debris floods, not only ordinary monsoon flooding.

For selected high-risk glacial lakes, direct interventions can also help—for example, carefully lowering lake levels, reinforcing or modifying unstable moraine dams, and coupling those interventions with locally managed warning systems. Nepal has already implemented lake-lowering and community early-warning measures at Imja Tsho in the Everest region, demonstrating that targeted mitigation is possible.

Was the glacier that triggered the event considered vulnerable and how do researchers assess glaciers?

At this early stage, it is more accurate to say that the glacierized slope was demonstrably hazardous than to imply that the precise failure was fully predictable. Researchers assess vulnerability by examining satellite imagery and aerial data, glacier retreat and surface changes, slope angles, fractures and crevasses, rock and ice volumes, evidence of permafrost thaw, nearby lakes, drainage pathways, and the likely consequences for people and infrastructure downstream.

Researchers assess the vulnerability of glaciers and glacial lakes, using satellite imagery to map their size, evolution, and growth over time. This helps identify which lakes are expanding rapidly and are therefore potentially dangerous.

Pratik Singh Thakuri, a Ph.D. student in my lab also from Nepal, has been actively acquiring and analyzing satellite imagery to better understand both the physical processes that drove this event and the extent of resulting damages. Trained as a water resources engineer, he focuses his research on modeling floods and other extreme hydrologic events. His work provides an important connection between remote-sensing observations of this disaster and the broader effort to understand, model, and reduce flood risks.

Pratik’s comparison of satellite-based images, from Aug. 24 and Aug. 26, 2026, look at the two scenes over the same geographic area, comparing the glaciers, surrounding slopes, avalanche pathways, valley floods, and downstream river corridors. By comparing different time periods, scientists can piece together the development of an event and ascertain whether there were any visual changes in the glacier or adjacent region prior to the event. Although this does not identify the cause of the event, it represents an important starting point for analyzing it.

When possible, teams conduct on-the-ground surveys to study glacial conditions, measure lake depth, assess the stability of moraine dams, and gather data for computer models. Scientists integrate data on lake size, surrounding topography, and downstream population and infrastructure to assess risk. A lake might be deemed "high risk" if a potential outburst could impact a populated area. We use computer models to simulate what would happen if a lake were to breach, predicting the path, speed, and volume of a flood wave.

The key question is not only ‘Could a glacier or lake fail?’ but also ‘Who and what lies in the potential flow path?’

There are other sites of concern in Nepal and across the Hindu Kush Himalaya. A 2020 assessment, by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development / United Nations Development Programme, identified 47 potentially dangerous glacial lakes across the Koshi, Gandaki, and Karnali basins spanning Nepal, Tibet, and India—21 in Nepal, 25 in Tibet, and one in India. These inventories are vital but need to be updated because glaciers, lakes, slopes, and downstream exposure are changing rapidly.

Could this kind of an event happen elsewhere and are there other areas that might be vulnerable or at-risk?

Similar cascading hazards can occur wherever steep, glacierized mountains contain unstable ice, thawing permafrost, fractured rock, glacial lakes, and communities or infrastructure in narrow downstream valleys. The Hindu Kush Himalaya is a major concern, but the underlying processes also occur in the Andes, Alaska, western Canada, the European Alps, Iceland, and parts of Central Asia. In a paper I co-authored in 2023, we discussed cascading hazards becoming more prevalent in the central Himalayas and how the need for an integrated modeling framework means more reliable prediction, with early warning systems essential for reducing impacts.

The specific hazard may differ by place. In some valleys, the major concern is a glacial-lake outburst flood; elsewhere, it may be an ice avalanche, a rock-and-ice avalanche, a landslide-dammed lake, a rain-on-snow flood, or a compound event involving several of these processes. Warming does not make every individual collapse directly attributable to climate change, but it is altering the conditions that affect glacier and permafrost stability in many mountain regions.

KATHMANDU, Nepal — Rescuers pulled two survivors from a tunnel linked to a hydropower station on Nepal's Trishuli River on Friday, nine days after a wall of ice, rock and mud tore ​through its valley, killing more than 1,300 people and leaving over 5,600 missing.

Officials and rescue workers say they believe the Aug. 26 collapse of a glacier on the upper reaches of the river trapped at least 900 people in tunnels related to six hydropower projects along the waters.

The two workers pulled from ‌the tunnel at the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station are the first to be rescued from the hydropower projects and have been taken to an army hospital in the capital Kathmandu, giving search teams a flicker of hope as the ⁠possibility of finding other survivors fades. The army said they had also recovered a body ​from the site.

Videos released by Nepali authorities showed Kabir Maharjan being hoisted from ⁠a hole in the ground as bystanders cheered, then lowered onto a stretcher. His colleague Sanjay Sah was brought out on a worker's back, his face still caked in mud, before ‌army doctors fitted an oxygen mask and checked ‌his vitals inside a rescue tent.

Sah, a mechanical foreman, later described staying behind in a control room to help others escape after he ⁠urged colleagues to flee upon hearing news of the disaster.

"I was in the control room, so my responsibility was to ⁠save everyone's lives. When there was such a big accident, it was not right for me to run away," he said in a video recording shared by Nepali authorities.

Sah told rescuers he spent time reciting mantras (verses from a prayer) while he was trapped. He said he had been in contact with three or four more people in the tunnel, while others could still be alive deeper in its reaches.

Nepal's army said it recovered two bodies from a tunnel at Langtang Hydropower Station, and continued searching.

At least 1,287 people have been killed in Nepal in the floods that swept away houses, streets and schools in towns and villages near the border with China's ‌Tibet, the disaster management authority said on Friday. More than 5,080 are still missing.

China has put the death toll in Tibet at ​21, with 541 others listed as missing.

Rescue was a miracle

The two rescued men are now in intensive care at an army hospital and their vital signs are stable, a source from the facility told Reuters. Mechanical supervisor Maharjan cannot move his hands or legs, but Sah's injuries are not considered critical, according to an aide to the energy minister.

Amir Maharjan, Kabir's brother, said he has not received any news officially but has been told to go to the hospital.

"I have been hearing from the news that my brother has been found. The entire family is very happy," Amir said.

A small group of people had managed to escape from another tunnel hours after the disaster struck.

A team of experts in a WhatsApp group was guiding rescue workers in the search at the hydropower projects in what has become a valuable tool alongside helicopters and ​heavy machinery in the race to find survivors.

More search and rescue operations were underway around the Upper Trishuli 3A project, the Nepali army said. Rescue efforts were being led by the army and police, with assistance from ‌experts from India, ‌South Korea and China.

Flood losses estimated at $2.56B

Property, housing and infrastructure worth at least $2.56 billion were lost in last week's catastrophe, Dharma Raj Upreti, chief of Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, said on Friday.

Nepal will need to rebuild around 20,000 houses in flood-ravaged areas, Upreti has said, with at least 7,500 of those homes destroyed.

The disaster could result in commercial insurance losses exceeding $132.3 million, with hydropower projects accounting for most claims, according to a top official at one of the country's leading insurers. Eleven Nepali hydropower projects lie in the affected region and ‌in many cases, access roads and above-ground infrastructure ​have been washed away.

At least 583 foreign nationals were missing in the floods, Nepal said on Thursday, ‌many of them pilgrims and trekkers.

Australian disaster response ⁠specialists left for Nepal on Friday ​to join the search for survivors, as the Australian government expressed "serious concerns" for the welfare of its 36 missing citizens.

अपर त्रिशूली ३ ए परियोजना के आसपास आरो खोज आ बचाव अभियान चलि रहल नेपाली सेना जनौलक अछि । बचाव के प्रयास के नेतृत्व सेना आरू पुलिस के तरफ स॑ करलऽ जाय रहलऽ छेलै, जेकरा म॑ भारत, दक्षिण कोरिया आरू चीन के विशेषज्ञऽ के मदद मिललऽ छेलै ।

बाढ़िक नुकसान 2.56 अरब डॉलर के अनुमान अछि

पिछला सप्ताहक प्रलय मे कम स कम 2.56 अरब डॉलर क संपत्ति, आवास आ बुनियादी ढांचा क नुकसान भेल नेपाल क राष्ट्रीय आपदा जोखिम न्यूनीकरण आ प्रबंधन प्राधिकरण क प्रमुख धर्मराज उप्रेती शुक्रदिन जानकारी देलथि।

बाढ़ि सं तबाह क्षेत्र मे नेपाल मे करीब 20 हजार घर के पुनर्निर्माण करय पड़त, ओहि मे सं कम सं कम 7500 घर नष्ट भ गेल उप्रेती कहलनि अछि.

देश केरऽ एगो प्रमुख बीमा कंपनी केरऽ एगो शीर्ष अधिकारी के अनुसार ई आपदा के परिणामस्वरूप वाणिज्यिक बीमा केरऽ नुकसान १३.२३ मिलियन डॉलर स॑ भी अधिक होय सकै छै, जेकरा म॑ अधिकांश दावा जलविद्युत परियोजना के छै । प्रभावित क्षेत्र मे एगारहटा नेपाली जलविद्युत परियोजना पड़ल अछि आ बहुतो मामला मे प्रवेश सड़क आ जमीन स ऊपर क बुनियादी ढांचा बहल अछि।

बाढ़िमे कमसँ कम ५८३ विदेशी नागरिक लापता रहल नेपाल बृहस्पतिदिन जनौलक अछि, जाहिमे बहुतो तीर्थयात्री आ पदयात्री रहल अछि ।

ऑस्ट्रेलिया सरकार न॑ अपनऽ ३६ लापता नागरिकऽ के भलाई लेली “गंभीर चिंता” व्यक्त करला के बाद ऑस्ट्रेलियाई आपदा प्रतिक्रिया ⁠विशेषज्ञ शुक्रवार क॑ नेपाल लेली रवाना होय क॑ बची गेलऽ लोगऽ के खोज म॑ शामिल होय गेलै ।

Nepal Floods: Response Continues As Medicines, Supplies Depart for Hard-Hit Communities

By Tori Gordon

Over the past week, Direct Relief has delivered 484 shipments of requested medical aid to 42 U.S. states and territories and 27 countries worldwide. The shipments contained 9.8 million defined daily doses of medication.

Medications and supplies shipped this week included rare disease treatments, cancer therapies, fistula repair kits, cold-chain equipment, and emergency medical backpacks.

Major Shipments of Medical Aid Depart for Nepal Following Flash Floods

Direct Relief has dispatched multiple shipments of medical aid to Nepal in response to last week’s devastating flash floods, which killed more than 1,200 people and displaced thousands from their homes. The shipment, sent to local partner Mountain Heart Nepal, includes antibiotics, IV fluids, chronic disease medications, wound care supplies, and personal protective equipment to address urgent health needs in flood-affected areas.

Another shipment departed Thursday, Sept. 3, for Dhulikhel Hospital, and contains medical supplies, field medic packs for first responders, and hygiene items for displaced people. Approximately 21 tons of medical aid are en route or in process as part of ongoing emergency shipments to the country.

Gordon Willcock, Direct Relief’s Regional Director for Asia Pacific, is in Kathmandu, working alongside local partner One Heart Worldwide to prepare packages of emergency supplies, including gloves, solvents, and other medical materials, bound for Nuwakot. The supplies will support hospitals and the broader response effort, with some being helicoptered into hard-to-reach provinces.

In addition to medical supplies, Direct Relief has committed $125,000 in emergency operating grants to three local partners. Mountain Heart Nepal is using its funding to support mobile medical teams reaching areas cut off from care, Shanti Foundation is providing hygiene supplies, child-friendly spaces, and psychosocial support for women and children, and One Heart Worldwide is working to maintain maternal and newborn health services in the hard-hit districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading.

On the Ground in Venezuela: Staff Assess Earthquake Response Needs

Direct Relief staff, including Chief Operating Officer Craig Redmond, traveled to Venezuela this week to as part of ongoing emergency response on the ground in La Guaira and at hospitals and medical facilities. The visit included meetings with partners such as FundaciÃ³n Wayuu Taya, AcciÃ³n Solidaria, GREMCA, and the Venezuelan Red Cross, as well as Caritas and the Venezuela Nursing Federation.

Since earthquakes measuring 7.2- and 7.5-magnitude struck Venezuela on June 24, Direct Relief has shipped 24.4 tons of medical aid, with additional shipments currently in transit or being prepared for shipment. Direct Relief has also provided $450,000 in cash grants to six organizations.

Emergency Grant Aids Search and Rescue Efforts in Hawk Fire Response

In response to the Hawk Fire, Direct Relief is providing a $50,000 emergency operating grant to Washoe County Search and Rescue to support the team’s current response and recovery efforts.

The Hawk Fire, which began Aug. 22 northwest of Reno, burned more than 15,000 acres and prompted widespread evacuations. While the fire is currently 98 percent contained, search-and-rescue personnel continue supporting re-entry and long-term recovery efforts. Washoe County Search and Rescue also responded to the Bug Fire earlier this month.

The funding will help the team purchase a larger generator for its Mobile Command Post and additional NOMEX fire-resistant uniforms, allowing more team members to operate safely alongside fire personnel during evacuation operations.

The grant is part of Direct Relief’s broader response to the Hawk Fire, including coordination with state and local emergency officials, regional response organizations, and Reno-area community health centers to assess needs related to evacuations, smoke exposure, and continuity of care.

Operational Snapshot

UNITED STATES

Direct Relief delivered 421 shipments containing 1.2 million doses of medications this past week to organizations, including the following:

OneWorld Community Health Centers, Inc., Nebraska

Around the World

Globally, Direct Relief shipped over 8.6 million defined daily doses of medication, totaling 106,931 pounds, to countries including the following:

Mexico

Venezuela

Liberia

Nepal

Egypt

Ukraine

Bangladesh

Haiti

Year-To-Date

Since January 1, 2026, Direct Relief has delivered 15.6K shipments to 2,442 partner organizations in 53 U.S. states and territories and 90 countries.

These shipments contained 271.8 million defined daily doses of medication valued at $1.2 billion (wholesale) and totaled 3.1 million pounds.
